scope: The forks quadrant: the Chicago River main stem, North Branch and South Branch meeting at the datum origin at Wolf Point, and the three divisions of land they separate.
standard: No contour survey of the 1835 town site exists. The earliest systematic levels are the 1850s street-grade and Chesbrough sewerage surveys. Every land elevation below is a period narrative statement in feet, back-calculated from grade-raising records, or inferred from geology — so NO land elevation in this spec is better than 'inferred', and the generator refuses to emit a 'documented' confidence for any land vertex. The one documented surface is the water: the pre-reversal river was sluggish and outward-flowing with a near-zero surface gradient, standing at lake level through the whole downtown reach.

context.label: Zero
context.text: Z = 0.0 ft at the summer-1835 lake and river water surface

context.label: Vertical exaggeration
context.text: 1.0 and it stays 1.0 in the data. Total natural relief inside this box is under 6 ft. A vertical-exaggeration control may exist in a renderer, labelled, defaulting off — see docs/LIBERTIES.md L3.

context.label: The modelled box
context.text: 641 m square centred on the datum origin, 2.5 m cells (8.2 ft — inside docs/PLAN.md's 5-10 ft), quantised at 5 mm, which is 1/15 of the 0.25 ft the dossier asks for. Row 0 is the SOUTH edge and column 0 the WEST edge, matching the renderer's Heightfield sampler.

context.label: Measured relief
context.text: Land in the modelled box runs 0.003 to 4.295 ft above the water surface, and the channel floor reaches -11.714 ft below it. Measured from the committed heightfield, not asserted.

notes: The water surface is the plane Z = 0 by the definition of this project's vertical datum, and terrain_gen.py emits it at a literal zero rather than reading this figure. So the mesh says exactly what this value says and does not say it BECAUSE of this value: change the 0.0 here and nothing moves. It is recorded because the datum has to be stated somewhere a reader meets it. The agreement is checked rather than trusted: terrain_inputs.RESTATES holds this figure against water_surface_m in the heightfield the bake wrote, converted from feet, so editing it fails the gate instead of quietly telling a visitor the river stands somewhere the ground does not.

Flat: the water surface is treated as lake level throughout the downtown reach and the river gradient as zero. WHAT ACTUALLY HOLDS THIS UP IS WEAKER THAN THE GRADE SAYS, and the honest statement of it belongs where a visitor reads the claim. No source read by this project measures the river's surface gradient. The sentence this `documented` rests on is one line of unfootnoted encyclopedia prose about sluggish pre-reversal flow, written in a section about the 1900 reversal. The regrade to `inferred` is queued rather than taken because a confidence is a mesh input and it lands with a Blender bake — docs/ROADMAP.md § S5, docs/STATUS.md § 45. THE PERIOD WITNESS IS DELIBERATELY NOT CITED HERE. Swearingen stood on this bank in August 1803 and wrote that the river was 'dead water' — but in the same clause he gives the cause, 'owing to its being stopped up at the mouth, by the washing of sand, from the lakes', which is the closed-mouth regime this project models as the epoch e1830_natural. This scene is e1834_harbor_cut: the bar is cut and the mouth is open, so his observation describes the condition that was removed. Attaching a tier-1 source to a claim it does not make would be over-grading dressed as a citation. See docs/RESEARCH/swearingen_1803.md § 5.

claims.label: channel_profile

fields.value: depth = bed_ft * (1 - exp(-d_in / e_fold_m)), d_in = distance from the waterline into the channel

notes: The e-folding distance is the river's. A watercourse may override it: the north-side slough is 7 m wide, and a 9 m e-fold would make a 1 ft channel 4 in deep and invisible.

The formula is written out here for a reader and implemented in terrain_gen.py, which does not read the string. The mesh does what this line says, and what holds the two together is one step weaker than a comparison: prose cannot be compared to Python, so terrain_inputs.RESTATES names the generator's own line and the gate requires it to still be there, exactly once, with comments stripped. A reformat fails it, which is the right way round — the sentence and the line are meant to move together.

The cross-section shape is a smooth approach to the reach bed and carries no evidence at all — no cross-section of the Chicago River at the forks exists for any date before dredging. It is under water and invisible; it is here so that the surface reaches Z=0 exactly at the traced bank line and so a boat draught question has an answer. Marked conjectural in the confidence channel.

The ground mesh carries one surface for the whole box — the renderer's earth colour — so the profile a visitor reads here, under the strongest confidence grade this project awards, is a statement about the site and not a description of the surface in front of them. What a soil section would change if it were built is the colour and texture of the ground, and neither is driven by this value.

The chip above this line is stronger than the evidence under it, and this sentence is the correction arriving ahead of the grade. The page was opened at its own locator on 2026-08-11 (docs/RESEARCH/surface_materials_south_division.md) and it prints no footnote, endnote or reference of any kind — its whole apparatus is a closing 'Further reading' line. Split by who says what: the ORDER — saturated sand lying on impervious clay, and a ground that will not drain in either direction — is attested by a named witness the page block-quotes, John Mills Van Osdel, Chicago's first architect, from having sunk building posts through the one to reach the other. The top layer of black loam and all three thicknesses, which are the only quantities here, are the 2022 author's own voice with nobody behind them. So a witness carries a third of this claim, the page will not say which document he is being reprinted from, and the rest rests on later scholarship alone. This is over-graded and the value is to become inferred; it did not move in the slice that found it because a confidence is an input to the ground mesh, which re-stales the committed GLB and needs a Blender bake — the same queue ground `water` is in, and the two land together. The two sibling entries carrying this profile north and west of the river are already inferred, on a weaker argument, which leaves the most scrutinised zone graded highest until the bake lands.

Inferred by the same extension as the north_division entry: the profile is stated for the business district and the dossier's surface-material table groups zones 8, 9, 18 and 19 under it. Two things weaken it here and are recorded rather than resolved. The dossier's own stratigraphic list maps the wet prairie west of the South Branch to the Equality Formation (lacustrine silt and clay), which is a different surface unit from the loam-over-sand-over-clay section; and the West Division is the one zone in this box whose ground is described as wet prairie carrying slough swales rather than as town ground. The grouping is followed because it is the statement that assigns zones, and the disagreement inside one report is the reason this is not documented.

citations.citation: "Wolf's Point and the Town of Chicago." Chicagology. Transcribing the Chicago Magazine of 15 May 1857 — the account of the Wolf's Point settlement built on George Davis's 1832 drawing and on Gurdon S. Hubbard's own description of the place as he found it in 1818 — with A. T. Andreas and modern editorial matter around it.

transcribes.work: Chicago Magazine, 'Wolf's Point' — the account of the settlement at the forks, engraved from George Davis's 1832 drawing and incorporating Gurdon S. Hubbard's description of Chicago as he first saw it in 1818
transcribes.note: Carries the Miller House's log construction ('a log structure partly sided') and the Wolf Point Tavern's ('partly log and partly frame'), the fact of a frame element on each, and — through Hubbard — the marshy river-shore strip that grades the south division's marsh surface in terrain_spec.json. Twenty-five years after the fact, from a resident's drawing and a named witness speaking to the writer: rung 2.

notes: The marsh strip IS in the ground — it is the dip behind the bank crest — but what it is made of is not: peat, sedge, reeds and rushes are the flora and surface parcel (S6), and the strip renders in the same earth as the plain behind it.

notes: The note below has said since this entry was written that nothing in the renderer is coloured from it. That sentence is a declaration now, checked against what the generator reads, and it holds for the other four entries too — which no sentence said.

Nobody in this project has seen this bed and no source record here describes it. The Cahokia Alluvium is the unit modern geological mapping puts along the river margins of this region, and the dossier assigns it to the channel zones (20-21 and the abandoned southward channel) on that basis, tagging the assignment inferred itself (docs/research/01-terrain-hydrology.md, surface-material table; the mapping it rests on is a modern geology reference and is not among data/sources/). It is a formation name carried onto this reach by regional mapping, not an observation of the Chicago River bed in 1835 — which is why it is inferred and not documented, and why nothing in the renderer is coloured from it.
